# The backend

Read `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` first — this skill is a pointer into it, plus
the procedure. `@langwatch/process` is the Node runtime **and** the
process-half vocabulary: `Server`, the container, `defineProcessModule`,
`defineRepositories`; `definePipeline` comes from `@langwatch/eventing`. An application (`apps/api`,
`apps/worker`, `apps/tasks`, and `apps/backend`, which hosts the api and worker in one process) is only
`main.ts` + `config.ts`; everything else lives in a module's `process/` package or in this
framework (the isolated `apps/scenario-child` is the one narrow runner). Full shape:
record §2, §4. In depth: `process-composition` (§4-§7) and
`module-dependencies` (§3.3, §6, §11).

## `Server`, the container, `boot()` (record §4, §5)

```ts
// apps/api/src/main.ts (abridged; the worker differs only in role and run)
const server = await Server.create("langwatch-api")
  .withEnvironment(processEnvironment) // config.ts: the one process.env seam
  .withConfig(processConfig(processModules)) // the installed list IS the schema
  .withSecrets((config, secrets) => secrets.withEnv().withFile())
  .withUpgradeGate({ role: "api", gate: servingUpgradeGate })
  .withTelemetry(processTelemetry("langwatch-api"))
  .start();
const app = await server
  .container("api")
  .exposeTransports((transports) => transports.trpc().rest().browserBundle())
  .boot();
await server.serve(app);
// worker: server.container("worker").boot({ classifyEventLogRetention }), then server.run(app)
```

`boot()` (record §5): the container opens the stores, orders installers by
peer tokens, and for each installed module picks the tier, checks each
registry's `requires` against the opened stores (refusal at boot, **by name**:
`"webhook needs clickhouse; none opened"`), builds repositories and channels
from the module's registries, resolves peers by token, slices config, calls
`<Name>Module.create({ repositories, channels, dependencies, config, secrets, role, resources })`,
then collects what the role wants (api → REST/tRPC/SSE/command senders;
worker → subscriptions, projections, process managers). The container
answers only stores and peers; every other "is it here?" is the module's own
answer (§3.3 rule 4), never a runtime fallback. There is no `withModules` in
an app: the `processModules` list is generated (`pnpm generate:modules`) from
`modules/catalogue.json`; installing a module edits the catalogue, never
`main.ts`. **The root never grows** — a change that needs it to grow found a
gap in the primitives; report the gap.

Tasks (`apps/tasks`) takes the `Server` for telemetry/config, skips the
listener; `server.container("tasks")` boots producer-only and runs the named
tasks, a module's own declared with `.withTasks(...)` (§5). A test passes no
server: `bootInstalledProcess({ role: "api", ... })` registers nothing
anywhere and returns the runtime for the test to drive (see Testing, below).

The shipped backend (`apps/backend`, `runBackend` from `@langwatch/process/backend-host`) runs the api
and the worker in one Node process, as `npx @langwatch/server` does; dev-runtime reuses the same host.

## A module's process half (record §3.2)

```ts
// modules/<name>/process/src/<name>.module.ts — the installer; the class is app/<name>.app.ts (§3.2)
export const <name>ProcessModule: PublishedProcessModule<"<name>", <Name>Api, <Name>ServerConfig> =
  defineProcessModule("<name>")
  .withRepositories(<name>Repositories)   // registry: { live, memory }
  .withChannels(<name>Channels)           // registry: { live, memory }; only if it has channels
  .withApi(<Name>Module)                  // the one class implementing <Name>Api
  .withTransports(<name>Rest, <name>Trpc) // inert declarations
  .withEventing(<name>Pipeline);          // only if the module owns events (§9)
```

No `.build()`; every `with*` result is installable. `index.ts` exports the
installer and transport declarations, **nothing else**. The installer is annotated
`PublishedProcessModule<name, Api, Config>` (`@langwatch/process`), an opaque type, so the module
class, repositories and generated database types never reach the emitted `.d.ts`; a test reads the
module through its Api, and boot still refuses a missing store by name. The installer lives in
`<name>.module.ts`, the module's identity (`modules/monitor/process/src/monitor.module.ts`); the
`<Name>Module` class lives in `app/<name>.app.ts` and stays thin, forwarding onto `services/`
held in private, `#`-prefixed fields, which carry the weight. `<Name>Module` never holds a
raw client, another service, or a peer's internals.

Folder grammar (linter-enforced): `services/` (one class per entity, never
opens a channel, never names a peer directly), `repositories/` (interface at
top; `prisma/` and `memory/` backends; only `repositories/prisma/**` names
Prisma, `PrismaRepository.for("Model")`, every project query carries
`projectId`; every ClickHouse query filters `TenantId` first),
`channels/` (messages to/from something the module does not own — bus, Redis
pub/sub, vendor HTTP, queue, email, Slack, SSE — one interface, per-tier
implementations, a memory twin, `{ live, memory }` registry), `eventing/`
(the pipeline, §9), `transport/` (declarations only, §8), `rules/` (pure, no
I/O). No `utils/`, `ports/`, `adapters/`, `composition/`, `lib/`, `helpers/`,
`domain/`. A raw client crosses into a module in exactly one place — the
`create(stores)` of one of its repository or channel registries, which the
container calls (record §3.2, §5). There are no members (§3.3).

## The four-way rule (record §3.3) — what a module may demand

1. **Derivable from supplied stores alone** → a repository or channel inside
   the module. No demand.
2. **Another module's capability** → a peer: the `*Api` token in
   `static dependencies`. The container resolves tokens; modules receive
   each other's implementations.
3. **A deployment fact** (signing key, base URL, admin list) → the module's
   declared config slice or secret handle (record §6); a process fact is a
   leaf the slice picks. Module code never reads `process.env`.
4. **An availability decision** (a capability this deployment may not have) →
   the module decides it from its own config and secrets, and its public
   config projects the answer to the browser. Off refuses by name with a
   stable code, or is a visible state; never a silent absence. Nothing
   outside the module answers it (no supply tokens; `.provide` survives only as a test stand-in
   for a channel-bound `*Api`, record §3.3).

```ts
  .mutation("create").withInput(createInputSchema).withOutput(<name>Schema)
  .build();

  .procedure("list").withPermission("<name>s:view")
    .handle(({ app, input }) => app.list(input))
  .procedure("create").withPermission("<name>s:manage")
    .handle(({ app, input }) => app.create(input))
  .build();

// a multi-status route declares .responds(...) (see api-transports)

    .withInput(createInputSchema).withPermission("<name>s:manage")
```

# The backend

Read `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` first — this skill is a pointer into it, plus
the procedure. `@langwatch/process` is the Node runtime **and** the
process-half vocabulary: `Server`, the container, `defineProcessModule`,
`defineRepositories`; `definePipeline` comes from `@langwatch/eventing`. An application (`apps/api`,
`apps/worker`, `apps/tasks`, and `apps/backend`, which hosts the api and worker in one process) is only
`main.ts` + `config.ts`; everything else lives in a module's `process/` package or in this
framework (the isolated `apps/scenario-child` is the one narrow runner). Full shape:
record §2, §4. In depth: `process-composition` (§4-§7) and
`module-dependencies` (§3.3, §6, §11).

## `Server`, the container, `boot()` (record §4, §5)

```ts
// apps/api/src/main.ts (abridged; the worker differs only in role and run)
const server = await Server.create("langwatch-api")
  .withEnvironment(processEnvironment) // config.ts: the one process.env seam
  .withConfig(processConfig(processModules)) // the installed list IS the schema
  .withSecrets((config, secrets) => secrets.withEnv().withFile())
  .withUpgradeGate({ role: "api", gate: servingUpgradeGate })
  .withTelemetry(processTelemetry("langwatch-api"))
  .start();
const app = await server
  .container("api")
  .exposeTransports((transports) => transports.trpc().rest().browserBundle())
  .boot();
await server.serve(app);
// worker: server.container("worker").boot({ classifyEventLogRetention }), then server.run(app)
```

`boot()` (record §5): the container opens the stores, orders installers by
peer tokens, and for each installed module picks the tier, checks each
registry's `requires` against the opened stores (refusal at boot, **by name**:
`"webhook needs clickhouse; none opened"`), builds repositories and channels
from the module's registries, resolves peers by token, slices config, calls
`<Name>Module.create({ repositories, channels, dependencies, config, secrets, role, resources })`,
then collects what the role wants (api → REST/tRPC/SSE/command senders;
worker → subscriptions, projections, process managers). The container
answers only stores and peers; every other "is it here?" is the module's own
answer (§3.3 rule 4), never a runtime fallback. There is no `withModules` in
an app: the `processModules` list is generated (`pnpm generate:modules`) from
`modules/catalogue.json`; installing a module edits the catalogue, never
`main.ts`. **The root never grows** — a change that needs it to grow found a
gap in the primitives; report the gap.

Tasks (`apps/tasks`) takes the `Server` for telemetry/config, skips the
listener; `server.container("tasks")` boots producer-only and runs the named
tasks, a module's own declared with `.withTasks(...)` (§5). A test passes no
server: `bootInstalledProcess({ role: "api", ... })` registers nothing
anywhere and returns the runtime for the test to drive (see Testing, below).

The shipped backend (`apps/backend`, `runBackend` from `@langwatch/process/backend-host`) runs the api
and the worker in one Node process, as `npx @langwatch/server` does; dev-runtime reuses the same host.

## A module's process half (record §3.2)

```ts

  defineProcessModule("<name>")
  .withRepositories(<name>Repositories)   // registry: { live, memory }
  .withChannels(<name>Channels)           // registry: { live, memory }; only if it has channels
  .withApi(<Name>Module)                  // the one class implementing <Name>Api
  .withTransports(<name>Rest, <name>Trpc) // inert declarations
  .withEventing(<name>Pipeline);          // only if the module owns events (§9)
```

raw client, another service, or a peer's internals.

opens a channel, never names a peer directly), `repositories/` (interface at
top; `prisma/` and `memory/` backends; only `repositories/prisma/**` names

`projectId`; every ClickHouse query filters `TenantId` first),
`channels/` (messages to/from something the module does not own — bus, Redis

skills.desc: Write or change a module's browser half (modules/<name>/browser): a screen, a drawer, a section, a hook, a slice of browser state, a cached read, or a data fetch in the UI. Use when someone says 'add a screen', 'add a drawer', 'where does this component go', 'browser state', 'global UI store', 'defineBrowserModule', 'stale read', 'cache this query', 'polling', 'auto-refresh', 'IndexedDB mirror', 'useUiDeployment', 'can I import another module's component', or 'ui/elements vs blocks vs sections'. Teaches the record (ARCHITECTURE.md section 3.4, 10, 10.2, ADR-169); for the typed data client see module-client, for components and tokens see design-system.

---
name: browser-module
description: "Write or change a module's browser half (modules/<name>/browser): a screen, a drawer, a section, a hook, a slice of browser state, a cached read, or a data fetch in the UI. Use when someone says 'add a screen', 'add a drawer', 'where does this component go', 'browser state', 'global UI store', 'defineBrowserModule', 'stale read', 'cache this query', 'polling', 'auto-refresh', 'IndexedDB mirror', 'useUiDeployment', 'can I import another module's component', or 'ui/elements vs blocks vs sections'. Teaches the record (ARCHITECTURE.md section 3.4, 10, 10.2, ADR-169); for the typed data client see module-client, for components and tokens see design-system."
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "<screen, drawer, hook or state question>"
---

# A module's browser half

Read `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §3.4, §10 and §10.2. This skill is the short
version. Exemplar: `modules/organization/browser` (screens, drawers, hooks,
features/ nesting, a colocated test). §16 says per row whether the new name has
landed; the declaration is `defineBrowserModule` from `@langwatch/browser`. The declaration stem stays `<name>.web.ts`.

## The shape

```
modules/organization/browser/src/
  organization.web.ts   the declaration; package.json exports ./declaration and nothing else
  model/                pure values and the module's *HostApi contract
  behavior/             hooks, the api binding, stores (organization-api.ts, use-*.ts)
  ui/elements|blocks|sections/
  features/<name>/      a feature owns model/behavior/ui again, one level, past 30 files
  testing.tsx           the module's test harness
```

Imports run one way: entry, then `model`, `behavior`, `ui/elements`,
`ui/blocks`, `ui/sections`. Elements and blocks take props or a query result and
never fetch. A section is where data meets layout. A feature that is one
component is a section, not a feature.

## Rules that matter

Each rule lives in the record; this table only points at it.

| Rule                                                                                          | Record |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ |
| Closed package: exports `./declaration` only; types cross, values do not                      | §3.4   |
| No kits: shared UI to the design system, another module's data to its `<name>-client`         | §3.4   |
| Screens declared with `.withScreens`, guarded by the router, never self-guarded               | §10    |
| Drawers are URL-routed singletons (`?drawer.open=<name>`); the name is the wire               | §10    |
| A screen expects missing data: skeleton in final shape, held data stays, inline Retry         | §3.4   |
| Four state tiers: React Query, router, the one global UI store (`<module>:<key>`), `useState` | §10.2  |
| Every read cached (React Query + IndexedDB mirror); no `staleTime` at a call site             | §10    |
| No polling, but two bounded exceptions (below); visible tabs stay live, hidden tabs make none | §10    |
| Deployment facts from `useUiDeployment()` or the module's `*HostApi`, never env               | §6     |
| Reads take an opaque id plus tenant scope; mutations `setData`, never hand-invalidate         | §10.2  |

**The two polling exceptions** (§10): a refresh interval the user chooses, off by default
(`modules/analytics/browser/src/behavior/use-dashboard-auto-refresh.ts`), and suite freshness
polling only while the live stream is down
(`modules/scenario/browser/src/behavior/suites/use-suite-run-freshness.ts`). Anything else is
a hint over SSE or a cursor-backed read.

Two habits the table does not show: a sub-flow passes `onClose`, never
`closeDrawer` (it clears the stack); an in-app link is
`@langwatch/browser-host/link`, never a bare anchor.

## Worked example: a hook over the derived client

The owner's client is derived from its contract and holds no handwritten procedure map. Clean
example: `modules/identity/client/src/identity-client.ts` (`createModuleApi<ContractApiMap<...>>()`
over the contract's declared procedures, never `AppRouter`). A new module puts its derived hooks in
`modules/<name>/client` (§3.4) and the declaration installs it with
`.withApi(client, { contracts: [...] })` (`installedModuleApis`, §10.1). Every read is mirrored to
disk by default (§10.2); there is no per-read cache policy.

```ts
const query = identityClient.<router>.<procedure>.useQuery({ organizationId }, { enabled });
```

No `invalidate` at the call site: a cursor-backed read goes stale through its key, any other
through SSE hints (§10, "A write makes reads stale through the key").

**Debt, not a model.** `modules/organization/browser/src/behavior/organization-api.ts` calls the
same factory but intersects the derived map with a 500-line handwritten one, and
`use-department-column.ts` hand-invalidates. Do not copy either; when a procedure is missing, add
it to the owner's contract and client.

A read takes an opaque id plus its tenant scope (`projectId`, `organizationId`), never a slug
alone. A query never returns a credential; a secret comes back only from a mutation. A mutation
writes the entity with `setData` instead of invalidating by hand.

## Worked example: a routed drawer

The token (`openDrawer(Token, props)`) opens it; the drawer mounts only while open and passes the
router's callbacks to the design system's callable `Drawer` (props in the `design-system` skill,
`references/component-apis.md`):

```tsx
<Drawer title="Edit score" onClose={onClose} onBack={goBack} size="md" footer={{ primaryAction: { type: "submit", label: "Save" } }} onSubmit={save}>
```

A sub-flow gets `onClose` from its caller, so closing returns to the caller; only the root drawer
calls `closeDrawer`. `dev/docs/best_practices/drawers.md` has the routing detail.

## Worked example: state and host services

One global UI store, owned per module and namespaced `<module>:<key>`:
`defineSlice` from `@langwatch/browser-host/global-store` (`persist` keeps preferences only, never
server data); another module reads with `readSlice` and cannot write. Example:
`defineSlice` in `use-dashboard-auto-refresh.ts`.

A host service has two shapes. A module's own `*HostApi` mount is implemented by the shell and
refused at install if unmounted. A **service the owner provides** is declared with
`defineBrowserModule(name).provides(Service, { load })` and read with `useHostService`; example:
`modules/feature-flag/browser/src/feature-flag.web.ts` and `packages/browser-host/src/feature-flag.ts`.

## Traps

- **Importing a router, `browser-host` internals or another module's browser
  package from a screen.** Read host services through their tokens
  (`useLent`, `useUiDeployment`, `openDrawer(Token, props)`) or the module's `*HostApi`, which
  the shell implements. An unmounted `*HostApi` is refused at install, by name.
- **A `queryFn` that re-enters the cache under its own key** hangs the query
  for the life of the page (§10, by-path dispatch).
- **Sharing by `./surfaces/*` or `./screens/*` exports.** Deleted spellings (§15).
- **Slots, `withCapabilities` for a peer lend, `useDrawer` by bare name, a
  per-module `use-feature-flag.ts` copy.** All in §15. Use a lent component (§10.1),
  `openDrawer(Token, props)` with the owner's drawer token (`navigateToDrawer` is the
  address door) and `@langwatch/browser-host`'s `useFeatureFlag(flag, { projectId })`,
  which keeps its name and is off §15's deleted list (§10.1, Alex 2026-10-05).
- **Host services are not "capabilities".** §3.5 reserves that word for the
  four layers; §16 renames the browser-host list to host services.
- **Any component built by hand.** A banner or alert, dialog, drawer, empty
  state, menu, picker or table comes from `@langwatch/design-system`; a missing
  need is added there first. Errors use the code-keyed presentation (§12),
  never `error.message`.

## References

Host wiring (host services, lending, `*HostApi` mounts, entitlement): §3.3,
§10.1 and the `frontend` skill. Layout of a screen:
`dev/docs/design/guidelines.md` §4. Specs: `specs/ui/ui-page-composition.feature`,
`specs/ui/browser-query-caching.feature`, `specs/ui/in-app-links.feature`.
Tests sit in a colocated `__tests__/` beside the code (§13). The module
anatomy: the `module` skill. The browser half has no generated page yet (plan
`dev/docs/plans/module-readmes-2026-10-06.md` §2); who owns what is on the module's own `README.md`.

skills.name: browser-pair
skills.desc: Iterate on UI with a person watching and giving live visual feedback. Pointer skill: the person uses their own tab on the stack and the haven orb; you read their notes and check fixes with `haven browser`. Use when the user says 'browser pair', 'paired browser', 'let's look at this together', 'open chromium', or wants live visual feedback on a UI change.
skills.body:
---
name: browser-pair
description: "Iterate on UI with a person watching and giving live visual feedback. Pointer skill: the person uses their own tab on the stack and the haven orb; you read their notes and check fixes with `haven browser`. Use when the user says 'browser pair', 'paired browser', 'let's look at this together', 'open chromium', or wants live visual feedback on a UI change."
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "[page-or-feature]"
---

# Browser pair: a person and you on one stack

There is no separate headed browser. Where haven is installed its gate refuses Playwright's MCP
tools, and `haven browser` is headless. The person looks at their own tab; you work from their
notes. `haven-browser` is the one authority for driving a browser.

1. **Stack.** `haven status` gives the app URL. If none runs, `haven up --agent -d` only when asked
   (`haven-lifecycle`). Tell the person the URL, and the mode: the default stack serves the built
   UI (an edit shows after a rebuild), `pnpm dev:hmr` serves Vite (an edit shows on save).
2. **Their feedback.** The haven orb on the page lets them point at an element or drag a region and
   leave a note. Read it with `haven orb feedback list --open --agent`, or block on
   `haven orb feedback wait` (`haven-orb`). Resolve a note once fixed.
3. **Your look.** Check a fix with `haven browser open <path> --lane pair --as admin`
   (`haven-auth` for sign-in). Use `snapshot --grep` to find controls and a `screenshot` when the
   change is visual (width, padding, colour, clipping, dark mode); a snapshot cannot show paint.
4. **Edits.** Read the component, make the smallest edit, say in one line what to look for, then
   tell them when the rebuild or save has landed. Components come from the design system
   (`design-system` skill); do not reach for raw Chakra.

Keep reports to a sentence or two: the person can see the page. Wait for their direction between
changes.

For a walk through scenarios with a pass/fail report, use `browser-test`.

skills.name: browser-telemetry-and-errors
skills.desc: What the small browser support packages are for and when feature code uses them: packages/react-rum (browser traces, error spans, navigation spans; the host starts it, features do not), packages/error-views (HandledErrorState, HandledErrorAlert, FormServerError, AggregateReadOnlyGate, resolveErrorCopy), the error presentation registry (now @langwatch/handled-error/presentation; packages/error-presentation is a deleted spelling), @langwatch/browser-host/errors (showErrorToast, applyHandledErrorToForm), and packages/design-system-internal (the paper look of internal consoles, not the product). Use when someone says 'show an error', 'toast the error', 'error.message', 'HandledError in the UI', 'form server error', 'field errors from the server', 'error page', 'RUM', 'browser tracing', 'browser.error span', 'react-rum', 'error-views', 'error-presentation', 'readHandledError', 'design-system-internal', 'console UI', 'haven hub styling', or 'aggregate read-only notice'.

# Browser telemetry and errors

Record: `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section 10.2 (browser telemetry, the paragraph "Browser telemetry"), section 12 (errors),
section 15 and 16 (deleted and renamed names). The component choice and tokens are the `design-system` skill; where a
browser file goes is `browser-module`. This page is the four support packages and the one rule that ties the errors
together: **a screen renders a failure from the code-keyed registry, never from `error.message`.**

## packages/react-rum: the host's, not yours

`@langwatch/react-rum` correlates browser traces with backend traces (ADR 058, `dev/docs/adr/058-full-stack-trace-correlation-browser-rum.md`).
It exports `startBrowserTracing`, `startBrowserErrorCapture`, `startNavigationSpan`, `NavigationContextManager`, the session
helpers and the constants (`RUM_DEFAULT_SAMPLE_RATIO`, `RUM_TRACES_PATH`, `RUM_SESSION_HEADER`).

- It is on by default wherever a collector is configured. Console errors, uncaught errors and rejected promises leave as
  `browser.error` spans through our RUM endpoint, which forwards them to the collector over OTLP and to PostHog when PostHog is configured.
- Two places depend on it. `@langwatch/browser-host`: `packages/browser-host/src/telemetry/browser-tracing.ts`
  (`useBrowserTracing`, fed resolved public config) and `navigation-tracing.ts` (one span per navigation). And `apps/ui`'s
  boot report (`apps/ui/vite/boot-report.ts`), which reads only the framework-free constants.
- **Feature code never imports it.** A module's browser does not start tracing, create a provider or add its own error
  listener; the shell already does. Throwing or rejecting is how a failure reaches RUM. Error text is sanitised and capped in
  the package (`sanitiseErrorMessage`, `BROWSER_ERROR_MAX_LENGTH`), so do not worry about leaking a URL query; do put nothing
  secret in a message anyway.
- Change it only when the task is the telemetry itself (sampling, a new span). It is a framework package.
- Tracing starts only once the app booted. Before that, the plain script in `apps/ui/vite/boot-report.ts`
  (inline in `<head>`) reports each first load as a `boot` span on the same endpoint: `langwatch.boot.outcome` is `drawn`
  (sampled sessions only), `stalled` (8 s still on the loading screen), `hidden`, `abandoned`, `reloaded` or `recovered`.
  Spec `specs/ui/boot-report.feature`. A loading screen says what it waits on with `<LoadingScreen reason="...">`.

## The registry and `readHandledError`

A server failure arrives as a `HandledError` with a stable code. The customer copy, title, tips and docs link for each code
live in `packages/handled-error/src/presentation.ts` and `remediation.ts` (record section 12). Subpaths:
`@langwatch/handled-error/presentation` (`explainAnyError`, `explainHandledError`), `/read-handled-error` (`readHandledError`,
`readErrorTraceId`), `/app-codes`, `/docs-url`.
`@langwatch/error-presentation` is a deleted spelling (section 15); a stale `packages/error-presentation/dist` may still sit on disk. Do not import it.

A new code needs copy: add it to the registry in the same change as the contract's `HandledError` subclass, or the screen
shows the generic "We've been notified" line.

## packages/error-views: what to render

`@langwatch/error-views` (`packages/error-views/src/views.tsx`) is the React half over the registry. It uses the design system.

| You have                                                | Use                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| a whole page that failed to load                        | `<HandledErrorState error={error} fallbackTitle="Couldn't load datasets" />`                                                                                 |
| a failed read or action inside a page                   | `<HandledErrorAlert error={error} fallbackTitle=... onRetry={refetch} />` (`onRetry` adds a Try again button)                                                |
| a rejected form submit                                  | `<FormServerError form={form} />` in the form's whole-form slot                                                                                              |
| text copy without a component                           | `resolveErrorCopy({ error, title?, fallbackTitle? })`: title, description, tips, docsUrl, traceId; `ErrorActions` renders the trace id and docs link from it |
| a screen that must be read-only on an aggregate project | `<AggregateReadOnlyGate isAggregate={...}>` (`modules/dataset/browser/src/ui/sections/datasets.screen.tsx:22`)                                               |

The trace id is always offered. Keep the data you already have visible beside a failed refetch; show the alert, do not blank the page.

## @langwatch/browser-host/errors: toasts and forms

Host services, not components (`packages/browser-host/src/errors.ts`):

- `showErrorToast({ error, ...options })` for a failed action with no form. Never `toaster.create({ description: error.message })`.
- `applyHandledErrorToForm({ error, form, hasFormErrorSlot })` places the server's `meta.fieldErrors` on the fields and, when
  none apply and there is a whole-form slot, writes `root.serverError` (shown by `FormServerError`). It answers `true` when it
  placed something: then do not also raise a toast. Example: `modules/agent/browser/src/ui/sections/workflow-selector-drawer.tsx:1`.
- `markHandledGlobally` / `isHandledByGlobalHandler`: a global interceptor already reported this failure; do not report it again.
- Alert versus toast: an inline alert for a failure that belongs to the content on screen; a toast for a failed action whose
  context is gone. One failure is reported once.

## packages/design-system-internal: not the product

The paper look (cream paper, warm ink, one orange, serif headings) of the internal consoles: the haven hub and stack home,
the IdP simulator, the mail sink, the mail room and Storybook chrome (ADR 160, `packages/design-system-internal/README.md`).
React and CSS only, no Chakra, no product design system. Colours, fonts, radii and spacing come from its tokens and
`styles.css`; a console writes no literal of its own. The product UI never imports it; the only consumers are internal
consoles, `packages/design-system`'s Storybook tooling, `packages/mail`, `packages/sim-console`, `apps/*-web` and the haven
orb panel in `apps/ui/vite/haven-orb/`. If you are writing a customer screen, you want `design-system`.

## Traps

- Displaying `error.message`: the tRPC wire message is the code slug. Render from the registry.
- Importing `@langwatch/react-rum` in a module: the host owns it.

# Browser telemetry and errors

Record: `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section 10.2 (browser telemetry, the paragraph "Browser telemetry"), section 12 (errors),
section 15 and 16 (deleted and renamed names). The component choice and tokens are the `design-system` skill; where a
browser file goes is `browser-module`. This page is the four support packages and the one rule that ties the errors
together: **a screen renders a failure from the code-keyed registry, never from `error.message`.**

## packages/react-rum: the host's, not yours

`@langwatch/react-rum` correlates browser traces with backend traces (ADR 058, `dev/docs/adr/058-full-stack-trace-correlation-browser-rum.md`).
It exports `startBrowserTracing`, `startBrowserErrorCapture`, `startNavigationSpan`, `NavigationContextManager`, the session
helpers and the constants (`RUM_DEFAULT_SAMPLE_RATIO`, `RUM_TRACES_PATH`, `RUM_SESSION_HEADER`).

- It is on by default wherever a collector is configured. Console errors, uncaught errors and rejected promises leave as
  `browser.error` spans through our RUM endpoint, which forwards them to the collector over OTLP and to PostHog when PostHog is configured.
- Two places depend on it. `@langwatch/browser-host`: `packages/browser-host/src/telemetry/browser-tracing.ts`
  (`useBrowserTracing`, fed resolved public config) and `navigation-tracing.ts` (one span per navigation). And `apps/ui`'s
  boot report (`apps/ui/vite/boot-report.ts`), which reads only the framework-free constants.
- **Feature code never imports it.** A module's browser does not start tracing, create a provider or add its own error
  listener; the shell already does. Throwing or rejecting is how a failure reaches RUM. Error text is sanitised and capped in
  the package (`sanitiseErrorMessage`, `BROWSER_ERROR_MAX_LENGTH`), so do not worry about leaking a URL query; do put nothing
  secret in a message anyway.
- Change it only when the task is the telemetry itself (sampling, a new span). It is a framework package.
- Tracing starts only once the app booted. Before that, the plain script in `apps/ui/vite/boot-report.ts`
  (inline in `<head>`) reports each first load as a `boot` span on the same endpoint: `langwatch.boot.outcome` is `drawn`
  (sampled sessions only), `stalled` (8 s still on the loading screen), `hidden`, `abandoned`, `reloaded` or `recovered`.
  Spec `specs/ui/boot-report.feature`. A loading screen says what it waits on with `<LoadingScreen reason="...">`.

## The registry and `readHandledError`

A server failure arrives as a `HandledError` with a stable code. The customer copy, title, tips and docs link for each code
live in `packages/handled-error/src/presentation.ts` and `remediation.ts` (record section 12). Subpaths:
`@langwatch/handled-error/presentation` (`explainAnyError`, `explainHandledError`), `/read-handled-error` (`readHandledError`,
`readErrorTraceId`), `/app-codes`, `/docs-url`.
`@langwatch/error-presentation` is a deleted spelling (section 15); a stale `packages/error-presentation/dist` may still sit on disk. Do not import it.

A new code needs copy: add it to the registry in the same change as the contract's `HandledError` subclass, or the screen
shows the generic "We've been notified" line.

## packages/error-views: what to render

`@langwatch/error-views` (`packages/error-views/src/views.tsx`) is the React half over the registry. It uses the design system.

| You have                                                | Use                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| a whole page that failed to load                        | `<HandledErrorState error={error} fallbackTitle="Couldn't load datasets" />`                                                                                 |
| a failed read or action inside a page                   | `<HandledErrorAlert error={error} fallbackTitle=... onRetry={refetch} />` (`onRetry` adds a Try again button)                                                |
| a rejected form submit                                  | `<FormServerError form={form} />` in the form's whole-form slot                                                                                              |
| text copy without a component                           | `resolveErrorCopy({ error, title?, fallbackTitle? })`: title, description, tips, docsUrl, traceId; `ErrorActions` renders the trace id and docs link from it |
| a screen that must be read-only on an aggregate project | `<AggregateReadOnlyGate isAggregate={...}>` (`modules/dataset/browser/src/ui/sections/datasets.screen.tsx:22`)                                               |

The trace id is always offered. Keep the data you already have visible beside a failed refetch; show the alert, do not blank the page.

## @langwatch/browser-host/errors: toasts and forms

Host services, not components (`packages/browser-host/src/errors.ts`):

- `showErrorToast({ error, ...options })` for a failed action with no form. Never `toaster.create({ description: error.message })`.
- `applyHandledErrorToForm({ error, form, hasFormErrorSlot })` places the server's `meta.fieldErrors` on the fields and, when
  none apply and there is a whole-form slot, writes `root.serverError` (shown by `FormServerError`). It answers `true` when it
  placed something: then do not also raise a toast. Example: `modules/agent/browser/src/ui/sections/workflow-selector-drawer.tsx:1`.
- `markHandledGlobally` / `isHandledByGlobalHandler`: a global interceptor already reported this failure; do not report it again.
- Alert versus toast: an inline alert for a failure that belongs to the content on screen; a toast for a failed action whose
  context is gone. One failure is reported once.

## packages/design-system-internal: not the product

The paper look (cream paper, warm ink, one orange, serif headings) of the internal consoles: the haven hub and stack home,
the IdP simulator, the mail sink, the mail room and Storybook chrome (ADR 160, `packages/design-system-internal/README.md`).
React and CSS only, no Chakra, no product design system. Colours, fonts, radii and spacing come from its tokens and
`styles.css`; a console writes no literal of its own. The product UI never imports it; the only consumers are internal
consoles, `packages/design-system`'s Storybook tooling, `packages/mail`, `packages/sim-console`, `apps/*-web` and the haven
orb panel in `apps/ui/vite/haven-orb/`. If you are writing a customer screen, you want `design-system`.

## Traps

- Displaying `error.message`: the tRPC wire message is the code slug. Render from the registry.
- Importing `@langwatch/react-rum` in a module: the host owns it.
- Two copies of the form helper: `modules/auth/browser/src/model/apply-handled-error-to-form.ts` restates the host's
  `applyHandledErrorToForm`; prefer the host's in new code.

---
name: browser-test
description: "Check that a feature works by walking its scenarios in a real browser and writing a pass/fail report with evidence. A recipe over `haven browser`: no test files, no browser commands of its own. Use when someone says 'browser test', 'verify this in the browser', 'walk the scenarios', 'check the feature live', or hands you a specs/*.feature file to confirm on a running stack."
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "[feature description or feature-file-path]"
---

# Browser test: walk the scenarios, report the evidence

This skill is the recipe from "scenarios" to "report". It does not drive the browser itself.
**`haven browser` is the one way to drive a browser** (see `haven-browser`; sign-in is `--as admin`,
see `haven-auth`; seeded logins are `haven-seed`). Playwright's MCP tools and `playwright-cli` are
refused where haven is installed, and MCP browser tools are never used by lanes. Use plain
Playwright only for something haven cannot reach, and say so in the report.

## 1. Prepare

- A feature file path: read it and turn each scenario into a numbered step with an expected
  result. A plain description: use it as the one step list. Neither: smoke test (app loads,
  admin sign-in works, the dashboard renders).
- Stack: `haven status`. If none runs, start one only when asked (`haven-lifecycle`), and say if you
  did. The base URL is whatever `haven status` prints; use that one origin for the whole run. A
  different hostname for the same app (`127.0.0.1`, say) fails sign-in with a 403.
- A plain `pnpm dev` stack serves the built UI; `pnpm dev:hmr` serves Vite. First loads can take
  tens of seconds under Vite.
- Workspace: `browser-tests/<feature>/<YYYY-MM-DD>/` (gitignored; never commit it).

## 2. Seed only what the steps need

Decide which data must exist (a suite with one scenario, one trace, a completed run). Create it
through the UI where practical; use the API or a seed (`haven db seed`, `haven-seed`) for bulk
data. Keep it minimal. Credentials for ingestion come from a seeded login or a personal scoped
key, never a project key read from settings, and never pasted into a prompt or a report.

## 3. Walk it

Use one lane per run (`--lane bt-<feature> --as admin`). For each step: act, check the expected
result in the diff or a `snapshot --grep`, and record PASS or FAIL.

- Take a screenshot for each step that checks how something looks (drawer width, card padding,
  colour, clipping, dark mode) and for every failure. A snapshot finds controls; it cannot show
  paint. Save with `--out browser-tests/<feature>/<date>/NN-name.png`.
- On a failure: screenshot, `haven browser console --level error`, `haven browser network --failed`,
  mark it FAIL and go on. Do not debug the app or edit code during the walk.
- Overlays are a routed singleton with a back stack: assert that one overlay is open, that back
  returns to the caller and that a draft survives. Two stacked copies of the same drawer is a
  defect to report, not a quirk to press Escape past.
- Waits are `--wait-for 'text=...'`, never sleeps. Close the lane when done.

## 4. Report

Write `browser-tests/<feature>/<date>/report.md`:

```markdown
# Browser test: <feature>

**Date / stack URL / branch / PR (if known)**

| #   | Scenario | Result | Evidence    |
| --- | -------- | ------ | ----------- |
| 1   | <name>   | PASS   | 01-name.png |

## Failures

- **2:** expected X, saw Y (console and network lines).
```

Return the table to the caller. Publishing is a separate act, done only when asked: upload
screenshots with `gh issue comment --attach file#alt` (see the repository's PR rules) and put
the table in a PR comment, not the squash-merge body.

## Rules

- Never ask the user for a port, account or browser: resolve them as above.
- Read `HOW_TO.md` beside this file for gotchas before the first run.
- Do not create test files. To turn a walk into an e2e test use `haven browser record`
  (`haven-browser`), then `record export`.
- For a live session with a person watching, see `browser-pair`.

skills.desc: Build or theme Chakra UI v3 components, recipes, slot recipes and tokens INSIDE packages/design-system only. Use only when editing files under packages/design-system. Feature code in modules/*/browser or apps/ui never imports Chakra: use the design-system skill instead.
skills.body:
---
name: chakra-ui-builder
description: "Build or theme Chakra UI v3 components, recipes, slot recipes and tokens INSIDE packages/design-system only. Use only when editing files under packages/design-system. Feature code in modules/*/browser or apps/ui never imports Chakra: use the design-system skill instead."
---

# Chakra UI Builder

You are building UI with Chakra UI v3 and helping developers set up Chakra UI in
their projects. Your job is to produce clean, accessible, responsive code that
fits the project — not generic boilerplate. Read the project context first, then
build or set up.

---

## Scope

This skill is for **implementation work inside `packages/design-system`**: a component, a
recipe or a token. A module or app never imports Chakra; it takes a component from
`@langwatch/design-system/<subpath>` (see the `design-system` skill). Raw Chakra examples below
are implementation-only: never copy them into `modules/*/browser` or `apps/ui`.

## Step 1: Read the project context

The setup already exists. Do not install Chakra, run the CLI snippet generator or write a
second provider and theme.

- Provider: `packages/design-system/src/provider/index.tsx`; the Vite composition root is
  `apps/ui/src/main.tsx`.
- System, tokens and recipes: `packages/design-system/src/system/config.ts` and
  `create-system.ts`. Change tokens there; do not add a `theme.ts` beside it.
- Components: `packages/design-system/src/components/<concern>/` (`forms`, `layout`, `overlays`,
  `display`, `states`, ...), each with a story and a subpath in `package.json` `exports`.
- Drawer, Dialog and Card are callable shapes with closed props; build with them, not from raw
  parts (`design-system` skill, `references/component-apis.md`).
- The app is a Vite SPA on Chakra v3. There is no Next.js, no `"use client"`, no `next/link`.

If the requirements are vague or the choices matter (layout direction, data shape, variants), ask
before building.

---

## Step 2: Choose the right layout primitives

Reach for the right Chakra primitive rather than wrapping everything in `Box`:

| Need                     | Use                                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Vertical stack of items  | `Stack` (default) or `VStack`                                                                   |
| Horizontal row           | `HStack` or `Flex`                                                                              |
| CSS Grid                 | `Grid` + `GridItem`                                                                             |
| Equal-column grid        | `SimpleGrid columns={N}`                                                                        |
| Centered page content    | the product layout component (`PageLayout`), or `Container` with a size from `system/config.ts` |
| Full flexbox control     | `Flex` with explicit props                                                                      |
| Semantic section/article | `Box as="section"` / `Box as="article"`                                                         |

Avoid deep nesting. If you're three `Box` levels deep with no semantic reason,
flatten it. Prefer `gap` over margin between siblings.

---

## Step 3: Use tokens, not raw values

Chakra v3 ships semantic tokens that automatically adapt to light/dark mode.
Prefer them over hard-coded palette values — they make the component theme-aware
without any extra work.

```tsx
// Prefer semantic tokens
<Box bg="bg.subtle" color="fg" borderColor="border.subtle" />
<Text color="fg.muted" />
<Box shadow="md" rounded="lg" />

// Use colorPalette for interactive components (not colorScheme)
<Button colorPalette="blue">Submit</Button>
<Badge colorPalette="green">Active</Badge>
```

Inside the design system, raw palette values (`blue.500`) are allowed only when a specific
colour is intentional and should not shift with colour mode, and new colours are made as
semantic tokens in `system/config.ts` with a light and a dark value. The foreground token is
`fg` (`fg.DEFAULT` in the config), not `fg.default`. Outside the package, only semantic tokens.

---

## Step 4: Responsive styles

Chakra uses mobile-first breakpoints. Use array or object syntax consistently:

```tsx
// Array: [base, sm, md, lg, xl]
<Box px={[4, 6, 8]} fontSize={["sm", "md", "lg"]} />

// Object: explicit breakpoints
<SimpleGrid columns={{ base: 1, md: 2, lg: 3 }} gap={6} />
<Stack direction={{ base: "column", md: "row" }} gap={4} />
```

Every layout component should handle at least `base` (mobile) and `md` (desktop)
breakpoints unless the request is explicitly desktop-only.

---

## Step 5: Forms

Use `Field.Root` for all form fields — it wires up label, input, error, and help
text correctly:

```tsx
<Field.Root invalid={!!error} required>
  <Field.Label>Email address</Field.Label>
  <Input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" />
  <Field.ErrorText>{error}</Field.ErrorText>
  <Field.HelperText>We'll never share your email.</Field.HelperText>
</Field.Root>
```

For form submission state, use `disabled` (not `isDisabled`) on inputs and
buttons. Group related fields in a `Stack gap={4}`.

---

## Step 6: Accessibility

Chakra's built-in components handle most accessibility automatically — don't
override it. The things you do need to provide:

- **Icon-only buttons**: always add `aria-label`
  ```tsx
  <IconButton aria-label="Close dialog">
    <CloseIcon />
  </IconButton>
  ```
- **Images**: always pass meaningful `alt` text (or `alt=""` for decorative)
- **Form labels**: use `Field.Label` or ensure `htmlFor` matches the input `id`
- **Interactive custom elements**: if you build something with `onClick` on a
  `Box`, use `as="button"` or an actual `<button>` so keyboard navigation works
- **Semantic headings**: use `h1`–`h6` hierarchy; don't skip levels
- **Color contrast**: don't use light gray text on white backgrounds; rely on
  semantic tokens which are contrast-tested

---

## Step 7: When to extract components, use recipes, and customize the theme

Extract a component when the same structure appears more than twice, or when a
piece is complex enough that naming it makes the parent clearer.

Suggest a **recipe** when a component has meaningful style variants that a
developer would want to customize. Suggest a **slot recipe** for components with
multiple coordinated parts (card with header/body/footer, stat with
label/value/icon, etc.).

For deeper theming work: defining brand color tokens, semantic tokens with dark
mode values, full recipe/slot-recipe authoring, typegen, or ejecting the default
theme — read `references/theming.md` before responding. It covers the complete
`defineConfig` / `createSystem` API with full examples.

For any chart request (bar charts, area charts, line charts, pie/donut charts,
`BarList`, `BarSegment`, or anything involving `@chakra-ui/charts`) read
`references/charts.md` before responding. It covers the `useChart` hook, all
three chart types, Recharts integration, color tokens, and complete runnable
examples.

When you're unsure which component to use, or the user hasn't specified one,
read `references/component-decision-tree.md`. It covers every Chakra component
with guidance on when to choose one over a similar alternative.

---

## Output format

Produce:

1. **Complete, runnable code** — correct imports, no placeholders like `TODO` or
   `...rest of component`
2. **Proper import statements** — group Chakra imports, then local imports
3. **Component separation** — split into multiple components/files if the
   component is complex or contains clearly separable parts
4. **Responsive styles** — at minimum `base` and `md` breakpoints for layout
5. **Brief explanation after the code** — 2–4 sentences on the key decisions
   made (layout approach, accessibility choices, responsive strategy). Skip the
   explanation if the request was trivial.

```tsx
// Good import style
import { Box, Button, Field, Stack, Text } from "@chakra-ui/react";
// Then local
import { SomeLocalComponent } from "./SomeLocalComponent";
```

---

## When to ask first

Build immediately if the request is clear enough to produce something useful.
Ask first when:

- The data shape is unknown and it changes the entire structure (e.g., "build a
  table" — how many columns? what data?)
- There are meaningful design choices the user might care about (layout
  direction, number of columns, color palette)
- The user references files or existing components you haven't seen

When in doubt, state your assumptions at the top of the response and build —
it's faster for the user to redirect from something concrete than from nothing.

- **Images**: always pass meaningful `alt` text (or `alt=""` for decorative)
- **Form labels**: use `Field.Label` or ensure `htmlFor` matches the input `id`
- **Interactive custom elements**: if you build something with `onClick` on a
  `Box`, use `as="button"` or an actual `<button>` so keyboard navigation works
- **Semantic headings**: use `h1`–`h6` hierarchy; don't skip levels
- **Color contrast**: don't use light gray text on white backgrounds; rely on
  semantic tokens which are contrast-tested

---

## Step 7: When to extract components, use recipes, and customize the theme

Extract a component when the same structure appears more than twice, or when a
piece is complex enough that naming it makes the parent clearer.

Suggest a **recipe** when a component has meaningful style variants that a
developer would want to customize. Suggest a **slot recipe** for components with
multiple coordinated parts (card with header/body/footer, stat with
label/value/icon, etc.).

For deeper theming work: defining brand color tokens, semantic tokens with dark
mode values, full recipe/slot-recipe authoring, typegen, or ejecting the default
theme — read `references/theming.md` before responding. It covers the complete
`defineConfig` / `createSystem` API with full examples.

For any chart request (bar charts, area charts, line charts, pie/donut charts,
`BarList`, `BarSegment`, or anything involving `@chakra-ui/charts`) read
`references/charts.md` before responding. It covers the `useChart` hook, all
three chart types, Recharts integration, color tokens, and complete runnable
examples.

When you're unsure which component to use, or the user hasn't specified one,
read `references/component-decision-tree.md`. It covers every Chakra component
with guidance on when to choose one over a similar alternative.

---

## Output format

Produce:

1. **Complete, runnable code** — correct imports, no placeholders like `TODO` or
   `...rest of component`
2. **Proper import statements** — group Chakra imports, then local imports
3. **Component separation** — split into multiple components/files if the
   component is complex or contains clearly separable parts
4. **Responsive styles** — at minimum `base` and `md` breakpoints for layout
5. **Brief explanation after the code** — 2–4 sentences on the key decisions
   made (layout approach, accessibility choices, responsive strategy). Skip the
   explanation if the request was trivial.

```tsx
// Good import style
import { Box, Button, Field, Stack, Text } from "@chakra-ui/react";
// Then local
import { SomeLocalComponent } from "./SomeLocalComponent";
```

---

## When to ask first

Build immediately if the request is clear enough to produce something useful.
Ask first when:

- The data shape is unknown and it changes the entire structure (e.g., "build a
  table" — how many columns? what data?)
- There are meaningful design choices the user might care about (layout
  direction, number of columns, color palette)
- The user references files or existing components you haven't seen

When in doubt, state your assumptions at the top of the response and build —
it's faster for the user to redirect from something concrete than from nothing.

Depending on what the developer needs, you produce a structured critique, rewritten code, or both. Read the code and project context fully before producing any output. --- ## Step 1 — Orient and determine intent Before any output, establish: - **Chakra UI version** — check `package.json`; use v3 by default - **Framework** — Vite SPA here; the Next.js lines in this file are upstream notes - **Source type** — existing Chakra, plain HTML/CSS, Tailwind, CSS Modules, styled-components - **What the user is asking:** - **Review only** — "check this", "is this correct/idiomatic", "what's wrong", "review my code" → produce a critique with targeted fixes, no full rewrite - **Refactor / convert** — "refactor this", "convert from Tailwind", "clean this up" → produce rewritten code - **Both** — "review and fix" → critique first, then the rewritten code State your reading at the top of the response (e.g. "Reviewing as existing Chakra v3 code inside the design system."). If code isn't shared yet, ask for it. Don't review a description of code. --- ## Step 2 — Analyze the code Work through the code across these dimensions regardless of output mode. For review, they become findings. For refactor, they become the checklist of what to fix. **Accessibility** - Do all interactive elements have accessible labels? (`aria-label` on icon buttons, `htmlFor`/`id` on label+input pairs, `alt` on images) - Is keyboard navigation possible? (fixed widths, `overflow: hidden` on small viewports) **Chakra API correctness** - Are v3 prop names used? (`disabled` not `isDisabled`, `colorPalette` not `colorScheme`, `gap` not `spacing`, `open` not `isOpen`) - Are compound components used correctly? (`Field.Root`/`Field.Label` and so on.) Overlays and cards are the exception: a consumer uses the callable shape, not the parts. - Are there v2 patterns still present? (`extendTheme`, `ColorModeScript`, `sx` prop.) `useColorModeValue` is Chakra v2, but the design system exports its own (`@langwatch/design-system/color-mode`): check the import source, and prefer a semantic token where it removes the conditional colour logic. **Token and style usage** - Are hardcoded colors used where semantic tokens would work? (`bg="#f9fafb"` → `bg="bg.subtle"`) - Are raw hex or palette values used instead of semantic tokens? These won't respect dark mode. - Are there inline `style={{}}` props that should be Chakra style props? **Component structure** - Is there unnecessary nesting? (`Box > Box > Box` when one would do) - Is manual spacing (`mt={4}` on every child) used where `Stack gap={4}` would be cleaner? - Are the right layout primitives used? (candidate for a component or recipe) - Are there one-off style overrides that suggest a recipe or slot recipe? - Are prop types / TypeScript types present and accurate? --- ## Step 3a — Review output Use this when the user wants a critique, not a rewrite. Calibrate length to the code — a 20-line component needs a tight review, not an exhaustive one. --- ## Step 3b — Refactor / convert output Use this when the user wants rewritten code. ### Conversion strategy by source **From plain HTML / CSS** | HTML | Chakra equivalent | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | | `
` layout wrapper | `Box`, `Flex`, `Stack`, `Grid` | | `
`, `
` | `Box as="section"`, `Box as="article"` | | `
` | `Box as="nav"` | | `
    ` / `
  • ` | `Box as="ul"` / `Box as="li"`, or `Stack` | | `

skills.desc: Change the ClickHouse schema without breaking the previous release, which keeps serving on the new schema: where the goose migrations live, `clickhouse:<NNNNN>` numbering and the migration-order check for collisions, one owner per file, one statement per StatementBegin block, IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS on every CREATE, ADD, DROP, MODIFY and RENAME (CREATE OR REPLACE is exempt), why a variable-size column added by ALTER needs a DEFAULT, why down migrations stay commented out, partition keys and TTL, deduped tables and argMax, why a goose file never drops a table, a column or a materialised view with an inner table (a drop is an operator step), why a type change waits until old writers are gone, historic values by a background .withMigrations step instead of an operator comment, the `-- background step:` note on a mutation (MODIFY TTL needs materialize_ttl_after_modify = 0) and the deploy-time rewrites it never excuses (MODIFY ORDER BY, OPTIMIZE FINAL, POPULATE), a changed view under a new name, every ClickHouse target applied by `pnpm task upgrade`, keeping the LWQL catalogue in step, and the expand/contract recipes. Use whenever someone says 'add a ClickHouse column', 'add a ClickHouse table', 'change that column type', 'drop the old table', 'replace the view', 'backfill a ClickHouse column', 'MATERIALIZE', 'write a goose migration', 'goose number taken', 'Code 173', 'Code 241', or the migration-safety test named their migration.
skills.body:
---
name: clickhouse-migration
description: "Change the ClickHouse schema without breaking the previous release, which keeps serving on the new schema: where the goose migrations live, `clickhouse:<NNNNN>` numbering and the migration-order check for collisions, one owner per file, one statement per StatementBegin block, IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS on every CREATE, ADD, DROP, MODIFY and RENAME (CREATE OR REPLACE is exempt), why a variable-size column added by ALTER needs a DEFAULT, why down migrations stay commented out, partition keys and TTL, deduped tables and argMax, why a goose file never drops a table, a column or a materialised view with an inner table (a drop is an operator step), why a type change waits until old writers are gone, historic values by a background .withMigrations step instead of an operator comment, the `-- background step:` note on a mutation (MODIFY TTL needs materialize_ttl_after_modify = 0) and the deploy-time rewrites it never excuses (MODIFY ORDER BY, OPTIMIZE FINAL, POPULATE), a changed view under a new name, every ClickHouse target applied by `pnpm task upgrade`, keeping the LWQL catalogue in step, and the expand/contract recipes. Use whenever someone says 'add a ClickHouse column', 'add a ClickHouse table', 'change that column type', 'drop the old table', 'replace the view', 'backfill a ClickHouse column', 'MATERIALIZE', 'write a goose migration', 'goose number taken', 'Code 173', 'Code 241', or the migration-safety test named their migration."
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "<the schema change, or the migration name the scanner refused>"
---

# Change the ClickHouse schema safely

**The rule** (ADR-155; ADR-173): no release is a required stop (Alex, 2026-10-11); any install upgrades
to the latest image through every step. `upgrade` runs under a lease while the old pods keep serving, and a rollback puts an older image on
the new schema. (A one-release upgrade runs goose `up` on each target in one pass; a jump across
several releases runs goose `up-to` each release's last version in turn, `releaseSteppingApplier`
in `packages/upgrade/src/runner/release-stepping-applier.ts`, `specs/upgrade/stepping.feature`.)
Every change is expand/contract, and nothing is deleted automatically (Alex, 2026-10-11): a goose
file never drops a table, a column or a materialised view that owns an inner table; a drop is an
operator step confirmed in Ops once safe. Which recipe applies at all: the `migration` skill.

Files: `packages/clickhouse-migrations/migrations/<NNNNN>_<slug>.sql`, applied by goose in sequence
order. Read `dev/docs/best_practices/clickhouse-queries.md` before writing any query the migration
implies. ClickHouse has no foreign keys; the no-relations ruling (the `postgres-migration` skill)
asks nothing here.

```bash
pnpm start:prepare:db   # apply it the way a deployment does: `pnpm task upgrade` (the worker runs the same command at boot)
```

The root `pnpm clickhouse:migrate` is an alias of `pnpm task upgrade`, so it goes through the ledger;
raw `goose` does not, and the api and worker keep refusing until `upgrade` runs. `upgrade` applies goose on **every** target (the shared `CLICKHOUSE_URL` and
each private dataplane endpoint), then fails the release if any target failed (round 14). It waits
`CLICKHOUSE_MIGRATE_WAIT_SECONDS` (default 180) for ClickHouse to accept connections. ClickHouse is
mandatory: a serving process with no ClickHouse refuses (round 20).

**What a failed migration looks like.** goose runs once per target; a target that fails is reported
after the others have run and the run exits 1 with code `schema_failed`, naming the target (`shared`
or `private:<organizationId>`) and its error with the URL redacted. The ledger keeps one row per step
and target (`done`, `failed` or `pending`), so `pnpm task upgrade status` shows which target stopped
at which `clickhouse:<NNNNN>`. The retry is `pnpm task upgrade` again (or Retry on Ops > Upgrades):
every DDL statement is `IF [NOT] EXISTS`, so goose re-runs the failed file from its first statement. Other settings it reads:
`CLICKHOUSE_CLUSTER` (set, every engine is Replicated) and, in the reconcile phase, the cold-storage TTL variables
(`packages/clickhouse-migrations/src/ttl.reconciler.ts`).

**Numbering and collisions.** The step id is `clickhouse:<NNNNN>`. Take one above the highest on
`origin/main`, not one above your branch: goose runs only above the version a database is on, so a
lower number never runs there. The `migration-order` workflow (`cmd/migrationorder`,
`specs/ci/migration-order.feature`) fails a number below main's newest, a number main took while
your PR was open, two files sharing a number, and any change to a merged file, and prints the `git mv`
to a free number. Stepping (`goose up-to` each release's last version) does not yet refuse a later
release's version that sorts below an earlier release's last one (`packages/upgrade/src/stepping/`
has no such code), so the main-relative number is your only protection.

**One owner.** Every table the file touches belongs to one module;
`pnpm lint:architecture --policies migration-owners` refuses two. Split the file.

## The file's shape

```sql
-- +goose Up
-- +goose ENVSUB ON

-- +goose StatementBegin
ALTER TABLE ${CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE}.coding_agent_sessions
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS GitBranches Array(String) DEFAULT [] CODEC(ZSTD(1));
-- +goose StatementEnd

-- +goose Down
-- IRREVERSIBLE: the rollback is a DROP COLUMN. `up` is idempotent, so `down`
-- is deliberately a no-op.
--
-- To roll back, uncomment and run manually.
--
-- ALTER TABLE ${CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE}.coding_agent_sessions DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS GitBranches;
```

Every line is load-bearing:

- **`${CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE}` with `ENVSUB ON`**: the database name is deployment configuration.
- **One statement per `StatementBegin`/`StatementEnd` pair.** ClickHouse has no multi-statement
  query; a second statement fails the migration halfway, leaving neither shape.
- **`IF NOT EXISTS` / `IF EXISTS` on every `CREATE`, `ADD`, `DROP`, `MODIFY` and `RENAME`.** goose
  on ClickHouse has no transactions, so a half-run migration is re-run from its first statement.
  The scanner refuses a statement of those forms without it (`ddl-without-if-exists`);
  `CREATE OR REPLACE` is exempt, and a mutation must be safe to run twice.
- **`DEFAULT` on any variable-size column** (`Array`, `Map`, `Tuple`, `Nested`). Parts written
  before an `ALTER` are unmaterialised and decode as garbage without one: **Code 173** at read,
  **Code 241** at merge. The most common ClickHouse outage in this repository's history.
- **The down migration stays commented out**, under `To roll back, uncomment and run manually.`
  The way back is the previous image on the migrated schema, which expand/contract guarantees.

## Recipe: add a column

One release: a new column with a `DEFAULT` is invisible to every older release, because `SELECT`
names its columns (nothing here writes `SELECT *`).

```sql
ALTER TABLE ${CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE}.trace_summaries ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS Tier String DEFAULT '';
```

**Historic values are a background data step**, a `MATERIALIZE COLUMN` or `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`
run on the worker, never a comment asking the operator to run it (plan 6.12, the "ClickHouse add
column" row; the operator comments in `00034`, `00035`, `00062`, `00063`, `00076` are historical
debt, never a template, plan 3.2 K2). A mutation is asynchronous and rewrites parts: the step starts it, watches
`system.mutations`, and is level-triggered. Declare it with `.withMigrations` as a `data` step,
mode `background`, on the module that owns the table (the `migration-data-step` skill, which also covers pacing by the
step's own queue work and `upgradelab` runs in the `upgrade` skill). A goose file
that still starts the mutation puts `-- background step: <step id>` above it, naming the step that
waits on it (`00103`; the step `trace:track-updated-at-index-materialisation` only observes the
mutation, it does not start it); without the note the scanner
refuses it (Alex, 2026-10-09). The note excuses a mutation only: `MODIFY ORDER BY`, `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL`
and `POPULATE` are refused with or without it, because they run inside goose and block the upgrade.

## Recipe: change a column's type

Never `MODIFY COLUMN` to a new type: it rewrites every part while older releases decode the old type.

1. **Expand**: a new column of the new type with a `DEFAULT`, beside the old.
2. **Migrate**: dual-write from release A; a background step backfills history; readers switch in A.
3. **Retire**: the old column stays; an operator step in the owning module drops it once an
   operator confirms in Ops that old writers are gone.

`MODIFY COLUMN` that sets only a `CODEC`, a `TTL` or a comment is not a type change: write
`MODIFY COLUMN <name> CODEC(...)` without restating the type.

## Recipe: remove a column, a table or a view

Release A stops reading it. No goose file drops it (`drop-table-or-column`, above the newest
`langwatch@v*` tag): the owning module declares an operator step (`mode: "operator"`) whose run
drops it through the module's own repository, and an operator confirms it in Ops once old writers
are gone. The upgrade registers it pending and never runs it; Ops has no generic "start this
operator step" action yet, so until it exists stopping use is the whole job. Dropping an index, a projection, a
plain view or a materialised view that writes `TO` a table holds no data and stays allowed; a
materialised view created without `TO` owns an inner table, so its drop is refused like a table's.

## Recipe: change a view

- **Same columns, same meaning** (a fix to the body): `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`, or
  `EXCHANGE TABLES` for a materialized one. Never drop-and-create: every read in the gap fails.
- **Different columns**: a view replaced in place is destructive (plan 6.12, enforcement item 2).
  Create a new view under a new name and switch readers in release A. A plain old view may then
  be dropped; one that owns an inner table is dropped by an operator step, as above.

Either way the catalogue moves with it (below).

## What a new table must get right

- **`PARTITION BY` the time column** the reads filter on (`StartedAt`, `OccurredAt`, `StartTime`):
  partition pruning is the difference between a local read and a scan of cold partitions in S3.
- **`TenantId` first in the sorting key**: no other id is unique across tenants.
- **A version column** (`UpdatedAt`) on anything deduped, and reads that dedup with an IN-tuple
  (`GROUP BY key` + `max(UpdatedAt)`), never `LIMIT 1 BY` over heavy columns (it OOMs).
- **`argMax(column, UpdatedAt)` for sort keys** on a deduped table; `max()` picks a stale version.
- **A retention expression** (`_retention_days`, `TTL ... DELETE`) matching
  `@langwatch/data-retention-contract`; the TTL reconciler, run on every `upgrade` and not a step,
  brings it back into line (plan 3.2 K3).

## A migration that adds or changes a view touches the catalogue too

The application owns the LangWatchQL access model (ADR-159). The views and the source tables behind
per-tenant row filters are the catalogue in
`modules/analytics/process/src/rules/lwql-view-catalog.rules.ts` (`LWQL_VIEW_CATALOG`), pinned by
`modules/analytics/process/src/rules/__tests__/lwql-clickhouse-catalogue.unit.test.ts` (spec
`specs/lwql/catalogue-grants.feature`). A new queryable table or view without its entry fails CI; a
missing entry refuses a query rather than leaking one.

## The scanner

```bash
VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=2 pnpm --filter @langwatch/clickhouse-migrations test src/__tests__/migration-safety.unit.test.ts
```

It reads every migration not in `src/__tests__/migration-safety.baseline.txt` and fails by name,
with the fix:

| Rule                                       | Refuses                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `drop-table-or-column`                     | a `DROP TABLE`, `DROP COLUMN`, or a dropped materialised view with no `TO` table, in a file above the newest release tag                                                         |
| `drop-without-retirement-note`             | released history only: a `DROP` with no `-- contract: retired in <release>`; a note never excuses a new drop                                                                     |
| `modify-column-type`                       | `MODIFY COLUMN` to a new type                                                                                                                                                    |
| `add-variable-size-column-without-default` | `Array`, `Map`, `Tuple`, `Nested` added with no `DEFAULT`                                                                                                                        |
| `one-statement-per-goose-block`            | two statements in one `StatementBegin` block                                                                                                                                     |
| `ddl-without-if-exists`                    | DDL without `IF [NOT] EXISTS`                                                                                                                                                    |
| `live-down-migration`                      | a down migration that is not commented out                                                                                                                                       |
| `view-replaced-in-place`                   | a view dropped and recreated                                                                                                                                                     |
| `untracked-mutation`                       | `ALTER ... UPDATE/DELETE`, `DELETE FROM`, `MATERIALIZE COLUMN/INDEX/PROJECTION/TTL`, `MODIFY TTL` without `materialize_ttl_after_modify = 0`, with no `-- background step:` note |
| `unknown-background-step`                  | a `-- background step:` note naming no declared code step                                                                                                                        |
| `modify-order-by`                          | `MODIFY ORDER BY` (a new sort key is a new table)                                                                                                                                |
| `optimize-final`                           | `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`                                                                                                                                                       |
| `materialized-view-populate`               | `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... POPULATE`                                                                                                                                          |

The last five rows keep reads fast while the api serves through the upgrade (Alex, 2026-10-09).
